title: Adaptation (2002) is the most eventful and meaningful film i've seen

commenti.body:
Really appreciate your write up. This movie gives me the exact same feelings… it’s one of the most emotional films I’ve ever watched.

Like you, I don’t really understand the reading of the third act as being purely some meta in-joke. It’s far too earnest and has too much emotional truth for that alone. Yes, it does knowing engage with screenwriting conventions that Charlie has expressed disdain for throughout, but the whole film is (expressly and literally) about the process of adapting… of adapting a book, of adapting to other people, of how life is one continuous process of change and adaptation.

Charlie learns from Laroche the power of being able to let go and move on, just like he has done many times in his life. And he learns from Donald to adapt his self-hatred into self-acceptance.

It’s a beautiful film, incredibly clever and funny, but just so human and full of pain as well. I adore it, and I don’t think it’s ever really gotten the retrospective love it deserves as one of THE great films of the 21st Century.

Yes!! I didn't really see Laroche's contribution to Charlie's redemption, but he has the quote "You know why i like plants? Cause they're so mutable. Adaptation's a profound process. Meaning figuring out how to thrive in the world". I can see how some of that stuck in Charlie's subconscious and helped in his acceptance of leaving the old behind

Yeah I think Laroche’s contribution to Charlie’s character development is somewhat second-hand rather than direct.

In fact, the pairing of Susan/Laroche are kind of meant to be the dark mirror of Charlie/Donald. Charlie resents Donald because of his freewheeling way of being, whereas Susan admires Laroche because of it.

But Charlie comes to adapt to Donald’s way of seeing things, and Donald’s death becomes Charlie the author absorbing Donald’s philosophy and internalising it (is it any wonder ouroboros is a running theme in Donald’s script?).

The difference of course is that Charlie adapts to Donald, thriving like a plant adapting to its new environment. Whereas Susan, despite being so fascinated with the idea of adaptation, can’t grasp the ability to do it. And so when Laroche dies, instead of adapting, she regresses (the repeating of the phrase “I want to be a baby… I want to go back to being a baby”.) When adaptation is no longer attainable, she rejects it for the idea of renewal, which is not possible. Hence her downfall.

So to me, Susan’s journey represents the path Charlie could’ve taken had he not embraced and adapted to Donald’s way of seeing things.

I understand why you might be moved by a lot of the characters' arcs in this film, but I think you are missing that all that growth and change and catharsis is just fuel for the engine of Kaufman's very cynically conceived Orobouros.

Remember: you are watching the film that Charlie is writing. Charlie sets out to write a film where nothing much happens. Where people (including himself) don't change, they don't have any epiphanies, they struggle and are frustrated and nothing is resolved. But he FAILS completely in the third act, when all of a sudden EVERYTHING  happens all at once: he introduces a deus ex machina (Robert) and follows all of his conventional third act writing advice, characters change drastically (porn and drugs and violence), they have epiphanies (Don on "you are what you love"), suddenly the stakes are incredibly high, there is action, tension, there is a chase sequence, multiple people die etc. he wows us in the end, and in doing so, he fails to achieve his ultimate goal of an uneventful film.

here's the orobouros: in failing to write a film where people don't grow/change, Charlie fails to grow/change as a writer. But then that means the story is ultimately about a writer who fails to grow/change and so... He succeeds? But... In succeeding he fails... But in failing he succeeds... And so on and so on etc etc

So to me this is ultimately a very cynical film that is more concerned with (admittedly very artfully) playing around with philosophical aporia than celebrating beauty/truth in human experience.

Oh i totally get how this works. That's a kick in the gut (and i like cinical media). But i think it's because i didn't think the film we saw is the film Charlie wrote. It just didn't click. And if it was, i thought Charlie outgrew his concept of nothing hapening because of McKeen. Thus breaking out of the orobouros, and the film is the story of the film he went on to create (which we will never see). Mainly because i couldn't convieve Charlie writing that third act, and it was more of a meta commentary. Also bc of some other stuff, like Charlie detailing that the world is created and then there's Suzie writing The orchid thief (whereas in the film we see, it's Charlie). These seemed to me like little details sprinkled in to break the barrier between the movie writer and the real writer, but they differ enough from Charlie's script (from what we see) that i can't believe they're the same. However i haven't read Kaufman's word on this

If it's not the line, "You are what you love, not what loves you," it's the line "I suppose I do have one unembarrassed passion. I want to know what it feels like to care about something passionately," that does it for me in this film.

I am someone that is struggling to find the spark in life--that's everyone, at some point.  But even I understand that sparks die out.  So if I'm trying to find the one burst of energy, who or what is to say what'll happen after that?

I don't have an ongoing passion, ambition, want.  I drift through time periods in my life of depression, apathy, listlessness.  Just the other day I was talking on my channel about not feeling anything.  And as good as that sounds next to not being depression or crying in a puddle, it may be just as or more dangerous.  Because I'm a living organism.  I'm here but I don't know why.  The onus of finding purpose in the purposeless is one of the greatest weights (and failures) of my life.

After so much time of living an undedicated, undisciplined, unimpassioned life.  Then you find yourself harkening back to an earlier Kaufman character saying "When you are young, your potential is infinite. You might do anything, really. You might be Einstein. You might be DiMaggio. Then you get to an age where what you might be gives way to what you have been. You weren't Einstein. You weren't anything. That's a bad moment."

So I'm in that limbo of wanting to *want* to have a passion but knowing if I don't have it at this point, it's most likely not going to happen.  So then what?

***

*Adaptation.* is a brilliant movie.  And it can laughed off because of Nic Cage, because of alligators, because I also know what proboscis means.  But it strikes a few nails on the things that even the most blank people (myself) can relate to:

*  You can get too in your head.  You're not supposed to know everything about everything.  You're here, you have some brains, you know the essentials and you know that if you can "whittle the world into a more manageable size" then you can begin to get somewhere.

*  When you're "done with fish," you move onto something else.  Because it *is* that easy.  Because you move on.  Because you either adapt or die.  If you choose to adapt, you choose hope.  As Gore Vidal says at the end of *The Golden Age:*  “As for the human case, the generation of men come and go and are in eternity no more than bacteria upon a luminous slide, and the fall of a republic or the rise of an empire—so significant to those involved—are not detectable upon the slide even were there an interested eye to behold that steadily proliferating species which would either end in time or, with luck, become something else, since change is the nature of life, and its hope.”

You become bored, indifferent, apathetic because you're done doing the same old fuckin' things you've been doing for years.  That's a sign to move onto something different.  If you don't, you'll stagnate and sink.  You're only hope is to adapt and move forward.  If you still have a pulse, there is still hope.  If you do not have a pulse, your matter will change into hope for whatever life force comes after you.  There is a win-win in this scenario.

*  You can't be born again in this life.  You can't be a baby again.  You can't be new.  You fuck up, that's it.  It's written in your life history.  But it's part of your evolution, and whether it was fated or shit just happened and shit happens, it's part of the evolution.  And you are different.  That is what's supposed to happen.  "What I came to understand is that change is not a choice. Not for a species of plant, and not for me. It happens - and you are different."

*  It's just a flower.  In the end you are mortal.  You're replaceable.  You're here and then you're not.  Everything that is significant to you is significant to **you.**  In that very private, brief exchange, you can conjure up a life that no one else will, ever.  It is a gift given to those that somehow make it through, with no reason why.  And although you are just a human, you are self aware of the time you live in and the person you are and are becoming, and that will mean something to someone, and hopefully, most of all, to yourself.
